data.text/markdown: ← 4. Contracts

5. Pipelines and engines

Say the Monday report the sales team presents reads orders by city, which read the cleaned orders, which read the raw orders feed. A few hundred orders change every hour, and a bad row anywhere below ends up on their slides. Recomputing every layer each time is slow, and hand-written incremental logic ("process the rows where updated_at is newer than…") misses deletes and late rows until the analyst finds totals that no longer add up. Next quarter the platform team also wants the job on another engine. We'll keep a join up to date from its changes alone, stack transforms into layers that pass only their changes along, run the same checked plans on several engines, and look at how the model treats doubles, time and text.

Keeping a join up to date

Incremental view maintenance computes the change to a result from the changes to its inputs. A source piped into a transform is a node, and node.refresh() keeps it up to date with update rules proved in Lean. We write the query once, as an Ibis transform, pipe one source into it and pass the other by keyword. The sources are in-memory tables (StaticSource, from sverify.io); Delta and Iceberg tables work the same way (chapter 1 reads a Delta table).

data.text/markdown:
What is maintained, and what is recomputed

Filters, computed columns, inner joins (self-joins too), cross joins, semi and anti joins on equal keys, UNION ALL, ORDER BY and DISTINCT are maintained from their changes, and so are COUNT, exact SUM and AVG, MIN and MAX per group. Other aggregates recompute only the groups a batch touches, windows that share one PARTITION BY the partitions it touches (for inputs without ties), and bounded RANGE frames the frames it touches. Left joins (a left join's NULL-padded rows must be retracted when a match turns up later), LIMIT (it depends on row order) and the rest are recomputed and diffed on every refresh (the guide). Contracts work on all of them, and the result is correct; a recomputed node costs a full run per refresh. node.status() says which kind of node you have:

data.text/markdown:
A recomputed node's change, the difference between its new and its old result, still flows to the nodes that read it. The view is a table like any other: view.table is an Ibis table to query further, and to_arrow(), to_polars() and to_pandas() return its rows. Nodes are built from Ibis transforms, or from a SQL string with sv.sql(query) (the guide).

Delta rules in brief

Every row carries a weight: +1 for an inserted row, -1 for a deleted one, and an update is a delete plus an insert. A table with weights is a Z-set, and adding a batch of changes means summing the weights per row. Filter and project treat each row on its own, so their change is the same query run on the changes only (theorem Rel.zeval_add). A join pairs rows from two tables. If both change, the new result has four kinds of pairs:
old customers B new customers ΔB
old orders A A × B: in the old result A × ΔB: new
new orders ΔA ΔA × B: new ΔA × ΔB: new
The change to the join is ΔA × B + ΔA × ΔB + A × ΔB. Hand-written pipelines often forget the corner term. We'll apply the changes "delete order 1, update order 2 from 5 to 20, insert order 4" to the orders, and "insert cy, delete bob" to the customers, with the corner term on and off:

data.text/markdown: With the switch off, the pair "order 4 and customer cy" is missing, since both are new and only the corner term produces it. Phantom bob rows appear too, one with weight -1: the updated order 2 was paired with the old bob, and only the corner term cancels that pairing with bob's deletion. Lean proves the full rule once. Rel.delta generates the update plan as an ordinary plan that reads the old tables and the change tables, and Rel.delta_correct proves it computes exactly the change. Any engine can run it. In the update plan of our view, orders$delta and customers$delta are the change tables, with a trailing __weight column; old tables get weight 1, and the join multiplies weights (how it works).

On each refresh, substrait-check --delta builds the update plan (Rel.delta) and encodes each row's weight as the __weight column (Rel.weighted, with Rel.weighted_eval covering an ordinary engine). Sverify registers the change tables, runs the plan as one query, sums the weights per row and merges the result into the view. A batch is computed completely before anything is replaced, so a failure changes nothing. A change that can't happen, such as deleting a row that doesn't exist, is refused by the source, and neither the source nor the view moves:

data.text/markdown:
The theorems cover the Lean model. Randomized tests cover the rest (the JSON translation, the Python glue, the engine): they generate random tables and batches with NULLs and duplicates, and after every batch compare the maintained view with a recompute, as the button does. view.refresh(audit=True) runs the same comparison in production and raises AuditError (from sverify.errors) before applying a wrong batch.

Pipelines

Real pipelines are layered: cleaned tables feed joined tables feed reports. In sverify the layers are transforms piped from the one below, so the code reads in the order the data flows: orders.pipe(paid).pipe(doubled) is the same node as doubled(paid(orders)), and the other inputs of a layer come by keyword. Without a .write in between, transforms fuse into one plan, maintained as one incremental view. .write(sink) stores a layer, and the layers above read the stored table as a versioned source through its change feed. An intermediate result is computed once and shared, and only changes flow through the layers. The base layer carries the contracts of chapter 4, and their guarantees hold in every state.

data.text/markdown:
When the data breaks the contract

A refused batch stops the report until someone fixes the feed. For a few bad rows among thousands, you may rather set them aside and let the rest through. With on_violation="quarantine" on the transform (or on the source), the refresh sets aside the rows that break a precondition, with the reason, and the node runs on the others (quarantine and hold). A row is set aside when a row condition is not TRUE on it, or when another row shares its key: both rows of a repeated id go, so the rule needs no order between them. Every precondition holds on the rows that stay (Catalog.kept_sound in Quarantine.lean), so paid's proof holds as before. We feed a Delta table an order with a negative amount and one with an id that exists already:

console.name: stdout
console.text: clean: orders: 3 row(s) quarantined (2 × unique(id), 1 × (_.amount >= 0), 1 already published), 3 in quarantine at /tmp/tmpg7_8ppki/clean_quarantine, changes from orders v0→v1 (change feed), requires checked on 3 row(s), 3 row(s) quarantined, merge v3: +1 −1

data.text/markdown:
The refresh completed (outcome is 'quarantined'). Order 4 went through. Order 5 breaks amount >= 0. Order 2 is now on two rows, so both copies are set aside, the one clean held before included, until the feed says which is right. The rows sit in a Delta table next to the sink, clean_quarantine, with the reason and the source version, and clean_orders.quarantined() returns them. A scheduled job posts flagged.alert() to whoever is on call, for example as a GitHub issue:

The rest went through, and the node's contract holds on them. A fix upstream (an update or delete of the rows) releases them at the next refresh. clean now holds:

data.text/markdown: on_violation="hold" holds the node at its versions instead: the refresh commits nothing for the batch, says why (outcome is "held"), and reads the batch again next time. The default, "error", is what the buttons above do. A change to the schema breaks a contract in another way. Say the feed's owner lets id be NULL, and the next version has an order without one. clean was proved with id NOT NULL, so the refresh refuses, and the message names the column, the version and the contract:

console.name: stdout
console.text:
SchemaError: `orders.id` became nullable at v1, and the new rows have NULLs in it; `keyed` was proved with it NOT NULL. Fix the upstream, or handle NULLs in `keyed` (e.g. `.fill_null(0)`) and relax `requires`.
The schema of orders changed incompatibly; views ['keyed'] have contracts proved against the old schema: build the pipeline again.

data.text/markdown:
Why the guarantees survive every batch

Whoever reads base relies on its guarantees on the hundredth batch as on the first. paid's preconditions were checked on all of orders once, on the first refresh. After that only the batch is checked: row conditions (amount >= 0) on the inserted rows, and keys (unique(id)) among the inserted rows and against the keys of the rows the batch keeps. Theorem Spec.update in Compose.lean says a table's contract survives a batch under exactly these checks, and Triple.maintained says a contracted view's guarantees then hold in the new state. So base satisfies doubled ≥ 0 and is non-NULL after every batch without re-checking the whole table, and the Delta table it is written to records those guarantees with every version, for the layers that read it. The layering is Rel.chain_sound (DBSP's chain rule): when a view reads another view's stored result and gets that view's change as its change table, its own update plan is still correct. For a recomputed view, ZSet.diff_correct shows that new − old is a valid change to pass on. Each refresh brings the layers up to date upstream first and writes every stored node once per state. After a restart, building the same nodes and refreshing resumes each stored node from its table when the plan and the source versions match.

Your own source and sink

Say the customers don't live in the lake. The CRM team has an API that returns the customers who signed up after a given time, and finance wants the city report as a Parquet file on their share. A source you write is one method, read(since), which returns the new rows and a cursor for the next read. A sink is one method, write(change), which stores what a refresh hands it. Sverify numbers the reads as versions, works out what changed, checks the preconditions and decides when a state needs writing. We read the CRM with from_query, which keeps a high-water mark on a column, and write the report with a sink that keeps the contract next to the file, so a restarted job knows what it already wrote:

data.text/markdown:
The plain refresh saw nothing new, and the audit caught the row the cursor skipped and applied nothing. A source can promise no more than its reads do, so give it an assumes= that says what its batches rely on, and audit now and then. The rest of the toolkit, in sverify.io:
  • from_frame(fn) reads the whole table on every refresh and diffs it against the last read, so the change is exact and nothing is assumed. from_files(path) reads the files that are new in a directory. Subclass Source for anything else. A batch can be a whole table (kind="snapshot") or rows added and removed (kind="changes").
  • A sink's write gets a SinkChange: the rows added and removed since its last write, or the whole table on the first, with the contract to record. contract() reads that contract back, so each state is written once even across restarts; without it sverify remembers for the life of the process. sink_from(fn) hands the whole table to a function.
  • These sources have no metadata, so preconditions on them are checked on the rows, and they keep the table in memory. A restarted job reads them in full again and numbers its versions above the ones its sinks recorded. A table format with statistics and a change feed implements the full VersionedSource protocol, as Delta and Iceberg do.
  • Storage holds object store options, or a function that fetches fresh ones, shared by every table that needs them.

Engines and SQL

A proof is about the Lean model. Whether an engine computes what the model says is a separate question, and engines disagree about NULL join keys, NaN, integer overflow, the rounding of integer division and the order of ties. Plans come from one producer: the vendored Ibis producer, or sverify's lift of DuckDB's SQL (SQLGlot) for SQL strings. DuckDB (the default), Polars on its streaming engine and Spark 4.3 run plans, each with a proved profile, and sverify writes DuckDB, Spark and Snowflake SQL; Snowflake's profile and running plans on it come before 1.0. The engines has the details. Lean's reference profile is the reference, one of the profiles that refine the core, and the tests use DuckDB as their default oracle. DuckDB and Polars are characterized fact by fact, each fact with its evidence (the ledgers). DuckDB and Polars run Lean's written form of the plan, so what runs is what was checked, and their translators spell out the reference's semantics, whatever the engine's defaults. We'll line the engines up. Pick a query: sv.verify checks it once, and report.run(con, engine) runs the same checked plan on each engine:

data.text/markdown:
What to look for:
  • NULL join keys never match, because NULL = NULL is not TRUE. Each translator says so explicitly.
  • Integer division truncates toward zero, as in DuckDB's // and in Lean (-7 // 2 = -3). Polars' own // floors to -4, so its translator truncates.
  • NaN is one value, equal to itself and above every number, so NaN > 0 is TRUE. The next section covers doubles.
  • qty + 1 on the largest integer is where engines differ most: Polars' own + wraps around to the smallest integer. An integer that leaves its declared width is an error, and verify reports it beforehand with the bound to declare, so no engine runs the plan.

Choosing the engine for a node

A node doesn't fix its engine. The plan is the same everywhere, and node.refresh(engine="polars") (or "spark", a Spark session) picks where it runs; DuckDB in memory is the default. A node keeps its state between refreshes, so the next refresh may use another engine. Contracts checked on data take engine= too: @sv.transform(ensures=[...], on_unproved="check", check_engine="duckdb"). We refresh a fresh node of the NULL-key join on each engine:

Every engine returns the same rows, and the NULL key matches nothing.

Splitting a plan across machines

When a table outgrows one machine, its rows live in pieces, and the plan has to run piece by piece. sverify.engines.run_sharded asks the checker how the plan splits: what each shard computes, and how the parts combine into the plan's result on all the rows (Rel.shardSplit_sound). It runs each shard on Polars and refuses a plan whose result would depend on the split. We'll total each meter's readings, kept in two regions:

An integer sum splits exactly: each region sums its meters, and the parts add up. A sum of doubles doesn't, since each region rounds its partial sum, and the rounding depends on which rows land where. The plan is refused, and the refusal names the way through:

console.name: stdout
console.text: NotShardable: SUM or AVG of doubles: floating-point addition is not associative, so the rounding depends on how the rows are split (run_sharded(reproducible=sv.equivalent(floats="plan")) splits them anyway, within a proved tolerance)

data.text/markdown: With reproducible=sv.equivalent(floats="plan") we accept doubles within the bound the proof gives for this split (StdModel.sharded_near), and tolerance=True reports it per row:

Each meter's total is within a few units of 10⁻¹⁶ of the sum on one machine, and the bound comes with the result.

Routes: how a proof reaches an engine

A proof is about the plan under one semantics, the reference by default. report.run(con, engine, route="auto") and node.refresh(engine=..., route="auto") choose how it reaches the engine, and refuse the plan with the reason where nothing does (how a route is chosen). The route names the plan's class on the engine: exact (every result the engine gives, the reference allows), observed (equal under lenses the postcondition states, a float tolerance included), shim (after a proved translation) or refused. Before the plan runs, its preconditions are checked on the data. We take the join to Polars:
Route on Polars: exact; evidence tested at 2.1.0 (facts polars-null-keys; #2539)

The reference isn't the only semantics to prove a plan under. With semantics="polars", Sverify proves it under the Polars rules, the ones your Polars run follows. The proof then reaches Polars directly (native). It reaches another engine only by a route that carries it there, such as transfer, where that engine's choices stay within those of Polars on every option the plan reads. A native run on DuckDB is refused, since DuckDB's rules aren't the ones we verified under:

Route on Polars: exact; evidence tested at 2.1.0 (facts polars-null-keys; #2539) An explicit route on DuckDB: RouteError: refused on duckdb: not verified under semantics="duckdb"; route="auto" tries every route

A stored node also needs a rerun to reproduce its result, since its sink commits each epoch once. The sink states what that means: exact bits (reproducible=sv.equivalent()), or doubles within a tolerance, DeltaSink(uri, reproducible=sv.equivalent(floats=sv.within(abs=1e-6))), for a SUM of doubles, which Polars's streaming engine may add in another order each run. SQL for DuckDB, Snowflake and Spark

When the data lives in a warehouse, the plan goes to the warehouse. report.to_sql(dialect) writes the plan the report checked as SQL whose result is Rel.eval of the plan. Columns are positional (c0, c1, …), filters keep only TRUE rows (IS TRUE), integers are checked at their declared width and every ORDER BY says where NULLs go. Each engine's differences go through a Dialect:

SELECT
  s1."c0" AS "k",
  s1."c1" AS "doubled"
FROM (
  SELECT
    s2."c3" AS "c0",
    s2."c4" AS "c1"
  FROM (
    SELECT
      s3."c0" AS "c0",
      s3."c1" AS "c1",
      s3."c2" AS "c2",
      s3."c0" AS "c3",
      (
        CAST(s3."c1" AS BIGINT) * CAST(2 AS BIGINT)
      ) AS "c4"
    FROM (
      SELECT
        s4."c0" AS "c0",
        s4."c1" AS "c1",
        s4."c2" AS "c2"
      FROM (
        SELECT
          "k" AS "c0",
          "qty" AS "c1",
          "v" AS "c2"
        FROM "t"
      ) AS s4
      WHERE
        (
          (
            (
              NOT (
                s4."c1" < CAST(0 AS BIGINT)
              )
            )
            AND (
              NOT (
                CAST(1000 AS BIGINT) < s4."c1"
              )
            )
          ) IS TRUE
        )
    ) AS s3
  ) AS s2
) AS s1

A query verify does not prove, as qty * 2 without the bound on qty, is refused with what it needs. node.to_sql(dialect) writes a node's plan the same way. Snowflake: integers are NUMBER(38,0) checked against the 64-bit range, timestamps are TIMESTAMP_NTZ(6), every identifier is quoted, and interval-valued result columns are refused because Snowflake has no interval type. Spark and Databricks: the "spark" dialect targets Spark 4 and is also what node.refresh(engine="spark") runs. It assumes the session settings of sverify_spark.dialect.SPARK_CONF, above all spark.sql.ansi.enabled: without ANSI mode an overflow wraps around and a bad cast gives NULL. Spark answers several questions its own way, and the SQL spells out or refuses each:
  • / of integers is a double, so division is div. / of doubles raises on a zero divisor, as the reference does; a plan that asks for IEEE gets ±inf or NaN from a CASE.
  • CAST(9.3e18 AS BIGINT) saturates, and FLOOR and CEIL return integers. Each is range-checked or repaired.
  • SUM of BIGINT raises on an overflowing partial sum even when the total fits, so it adds DECIMAL(38,0).
  • TIMESTAMP is the session time zone's, and so is what date_trunc returns, so the SQL stays in TIMESTAMP_NTZ.
  • POWER of doubles is Java's Math.pow (within 1 ulp of C's) and is refused.
Spark runs locally, unlike Snowflake. The tests run every coverage case and every query of the Snowflake suite on a local Spark session (Java 17 or 21) and compare them with Rel.eval. The Lean evaluator is the specification: the suite runs every fixture and every update plan on Polars and DuckDB with random tables, and compares them with each other and with Rel.eval, row for row in Lean's order where order matters. The Snowflake SQL is parsed and run on fakesnow. The engine profiles list where each engine departs from the reference.

Doubles, time and text

Say one of your sensors sends NaN, or a timestamp lands at the edge of the calendar. Floating-point measurements, timestamps and strings each have traps, and the Lean model pins them down bit for bit where it matters, because a proof about the wrong semantics proves nothing.

Doubles: NaN, infinities and one zero

In IEEE 754 comparisons and in Python, NaN equals nothing, itself included. SQL engines (PostgreSQL, DuckDB, Spark, Snowflake) order doubles differently, and so does sverify's reference profile:
−∞ < … < 0.0 < … < +∞ < NaN
There is one NaN, equal to itself and larger than every number, and one zero: −0.0 is 0.0, so -0.0 >= 0 holds and −0.0 never shows in a result. Lean's core keeps both zeros and signed NaNs, and the reference profile reads them this way (core, profiles and engines). An order like Rust's f64::total_cmp splits both (docs/how-it-works.md). Here is a table with both zeros and NaN:

data.text/markdown: Two consequences. v > 0 keeps NaN rows, so a filter meant as "positive readings" lets glitches through, and only an upper bound (v < 1e9, say) removes NaN. And the table was given both zeros and holds one: DISTINCT keeps a single zero and -1 * 0.0 is 0.0, on every engine. Lean models doubles exactly, as integer codes in the same order, so the proofs know all of this. We build a filter and see whether "no NaN" follows:

data.text/markdown: Comparisons with constants are exact, sentinels like -9999.0 and the boundary between v > 0.5 and v >= 0.5 included. Arithmetic on doubles (v * 2.5) rounds, and the checker bounds +, -, * and / from their inputs' bounds with a proved rounding error (float bounds). The reference raises where an operation on finite doubles overflows to ±∞, so where no bound keeps v * 2.5 finite, the report assumes it stays finite and the run checks it on the data first: a ±∞ in a result came from the data. For the same reason power(-inf, 0.5) and a MEDIAN between −∞ and +∞ raise, where engines disagree. FLOOR, CEIL, ROUND and the cast to an integer are exact and monotone, so a bounded double rounds to a bounded integer:

data.text/markdown:
Averages round

A sum or average of doubles rounds, and each engine adds in its own order. Say every reading is at most 60. The reference rounds the exact average once, so its average is at most 60 too, and the claim is proved. An engine's average can land a few units of 10⁻⁹ above it. With a row cap, Lean bounds how far (StdModel.epsilon_avg_cr), and the route to an engine says how close the claim comes:

console.name: stdout
console.text: refused: agg.fsum's sum_order: the postcondition (_.avg_temp <= 60.0) reads avg_temp, which is within abs=6.66137e-09 of the reference: write it as sv.approx((_.avg_temp <= 60.0)), or state sv.equivalent(floats=sv.within(abs=7e-09)) in ensures (duckdb-sum-double, duckdb-avg-double)

data.text/markdown: The hint names the exit, sv.approx, which states the claim up to that rounding. With it the claim is proved, and the report's lenses: line says which results count as the same: the doubles within the plan's bound (floats="plan", the default of sv.equivalent):

Drop the row cap and the sum has no bound at all: with the number of rows open, Lean cannot say how far an engine's sum is from the reference's. A claim that reads only the sign of the total still goes through, since adding values of one sign keeps the sign in every order. A tolerance you state is another matter. There is nothing to meet it with, so the route refuses and names the exits, a row cap or floats="plan":

console.name: stdout
console.text:
verified under semantics="portable"; the translation to duckdb is sverify's DuckDB lowering, proved for every plan, and its SQL writer
not verified: ensures total ≥ 0.0 depends on floats, which the lenses ignore; no engine meets the lenses' tolerance on doubles: agg.fsum's sum_order: total has no bound on its distance to the reference, and the postcondition asks within(rel=1e-06): state sv.equivalent(floats="plan") or drop the tolerance (duckdb-sum-double, duckdb-avg-double) (see report.unproved, report.details()); run(..., unverified=True) runs it anyway

data.text/markdown: With sv.max_rows(1_000_000) in requires the sum has a bound (abs=0.0067, rel=2.2e-10). Now a claim about the value of the total, such as total <= 6e7, is refused with the exit sv.approx, as the average above was: the reference's total may sit at the limit where an engine's lands a hair beyond it.

Timestamps and intervals

Timestamps are microseconds since 1970 (UTC) in the model, and intervals are durations. Comparisons with literals, ts + interval, ts1 - ts0 and joins on time are tracked like integers. The calendar functions are computed exactly on the Gregorian calendar (Time.lean), and Lean proves they grow with the timestamp, so a range of timestamps gives a range of years and of truncated months. Pick a time window and see what Lean derives:

data.text/markdown: Within one calendar year, year is that exact integer. Truncations stay inside the window's range, rounded down, and hour is in [0, 23], a proved range that doesn't grow with the timestamp. Without the filter, truncating to a month may fail near the ends of the timestamp range, so the plan needs ts between 1678 and 2262, the range of nanosecond timestamps. Sverify works it out and asks you to declare it (chapter 4 shows how inferred bounds work):

Decimals, and the types sverify reads

Money is a decimal, and a scale that drops a cent is a wrong answer that looks right. Sverify reads each column's type and keeps a decimal's precision and scale through the plan: a price of DECIMAL(10, 2) times a quantity is still in cents. A type it doesn't model yet is refused when it reads the table, with the cast that gets you through. We'll load order lines whose ids came in as unsigned integers:

data.text/markdown: UPPER, LOWER and regular expressions are black boxes: Lean knows they return a string (or a boolean), and no proof depends on which one, because Unicode case mapping and regex engines are large and engine-specific. A regular expression is a possible runtime error unless Lean can see that it compiles. Patterns in a conservative subset of Rust's syntax are accepted, and anything fancier is reported. A back-reference like \1 isn't supported by Rust's regex crate at all:

data.text/markdown: Contracts don't track string contents yet: startswith('acc') in a filter doesn't let Lean prove startswith('ac') afterwards. Lengths, NULLs and errors are tracked. You can now keep a join up to date from its changes, stack contracted transforms into layers that pass only their changes along, and rely on their guarantees in every state while only each batch is checked. You can refresh a node on DuckDB, Polars or Spark, hand a plan to Snowflake as SQL, and tell where an engine could depart from the model. The next chapter, Running it in production, covers the work around a proved pipeline: checking its file in CI, testing it, its credentials, its lineage and a bound on its state.
